Many of the earliest bars are flat (open=high=low=close identical) with zero or near-zero volume -- these look like stale/no-trade marks on a not-yet-liquid or not-yet-front-month contract, not real price discovery. Real, densely-traded 4-hour data is really only available from roughly the last 6-9 months, not the full 2 years the date range suggests. This is an important data-quality caveat distinct from the raw depth cap: a longer nominal window does not mean uniformly usable data across that window. Not persisted to data/raw/ this pass (large, and quality caveat above means it needs the roll-adjusted continuous-series treatment from section 13 before use, not a raw single-contract dump).

MAJOR REVISION to the conclusion below, found after this file was first written: daily bars reach much further back than any intraday size, and depth varies hugely by instrument because it tracks how long that SPECIFIC contract has genuinely been trading (not a fixed connector-wide cap). MES front (MESZ6): ~250 real bars from 2025-09-22. MES next (MESH7): ~197 bars from 2025-12-22. MGC front (MGCV6): ~450 bars from 2024-11-28 (~1.75 years). MGC next (MGCZ6): ~440 bars from 2024-12-31. MCL front (MCLV6) AND MCL next (MCLX6): ~750 bars EACH from 2023-10-23 (~3 years) -- crude oil trades deep, genuinely liquid forward months (unlike equity index quarterlies, which only have real depth in the front 1-2 contracts), so even the 'next' WTI contract has real multi-year history. All still capped at 1000 bars/call with no pagination, so a contract trading longer than that would still be truncated, but none of these hit the cap.

critical_limitation: The get_price_history tool schema exposes no start/end date parameter and no pagination cursor -- only `period` (a fixed lookback from now) or `step_count` (a bar count from now). There is no way discovered so far to request an older window once the ~1000-bar cap for a given bar size AND that specific contract's own trading history is reached. Below ONE_DAY, this means the connector can serve, at most, roughly the MOST RECENT ~2.5 weeks of 5-minute bars, ~6-7 weeks of 15-minute, ~13-14 weeks of 30-minute, ~3 months of hourly, or (with the data-quality caveat above about sparse early history) up to roughly 6-9 months of genuinely liquid 4-hour bars. AT ONE_DAY, depth is much better and varies by instrument/contract liquidity -- see the ONE_DAY finding above -- up to ~3 years for WTI (MCL) front and next contracts.

depth_summary_by_bar_size.4hour: nominal ~2 years but only ~6-9 months of that is densely/genuinely traded; earlier bars are sparse stale marks (all 3 instruments)
depth_summary_by_bar_size.1day: varies a lot by instrument: MES ~250 bars (~1 year) front, ~197 next; MGC ~450 bars (~1.75yr) front, ~440 next; MCL ~750 bars (~3yr) front AND next -- crude's forward months are genuinely liquid unlike equity index quarterlies

conclusion: REVISED from this file's original conclusion (see the ONE_DAY finding above, added after further investigation): sub-daily bar sizes remain NOT sufficient for the multi-year 5-minute-to-4-hour academic replication and backtesting the mandate requires (section 8-11, section 17's chronological split needs years of data at intraday resolution). But DAILY bars are a materially different story, especially for WTI (MCL), where both the front and next contract genuinely have ~3 years of real trading history -- enough to support a real (if not yet multi-decade) daily-frequency test, which sub-daily granularity cannot offer here at all. Sections 8/11's specific intraday (5min-4hr) research questions still need an external vendor (Databento, CME DataMine, Barchart, per section 14) to test properly. Daily-frequency, longer-horizon hypotheses (e.g. the term-structure/carry mechanism tested in hypothesis_ledger.csv H003) are now within reach using this connector alone, at least for MCL.

second_revision_daily_bar_staleness.purpose: H009 (SESSION_DECOMP_v1) found a strong result on MCL's most recent 199 daily bars (intraday leg, t=2.43). Attempted to extend the test further back using MCL's full ~750-bar (~2.9yr) daily history to corroborate it, per user request.
second_revision_daily_bar_staleness.finding: 712 MCL front-contract daily bars fetched (2023-10-23 to 2026-09-11). 530/712 (74%) have open==close EXACTLY -- not genuine intraday OHLC, but stale single-quote marks, same failure mode already documented above for 4-hour bars ('sparse stale marks on a not-yet-liquid contract') but not previously checked at daily resolution this far back. Staleness is heavily front-loaded and decays smoothly: quartile 1 (2023-10-23 to 2024-07-18) is 178/178 (100%) flat; quartile 2 is 176/178 (99%); quartile 3 is 160/178 (90%); quartile 4 (2025-12-26 to 2026-09-11, nearly identical to the original 199-day window already used) is only 16/178 (9%) flat -- i.e. mostly genuine.
second_revision_daily_bar_staleness.implication: MCL daily bars from this connector only become genuinely intraday-informative (open != close, real session movement captured) in roughly the most recent ~9 months. Any strategy relying on the DIFFERENCE between a bar's own open and close (e.g. SESSION_DECOMP_v1's intraday leg) cannot be meaningfully tested further back than that using this data source -- attempting to do so does not add real signal, it pads the sample with structurally-zero measurements. Strategies relying only on bar-to-bar CLOSE levels (e.g. SPREAD_MEAN_REV_v1's z-score, or any close-to-close return) are NOT affected by this and extend genuinely (confirmed: H008 re-run on the full 712-bar window produced a legitimately larger, still-rejected sample of 42 trades vs. the original 10).
